A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with the same title, authors and three research questions. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on bias detection, fair model selection and bias mitigation using Civil Comments and Jigsaw, with additional results and analyses in its appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on sentiment analysis, vocabulary coverage, model alignment, computational efficiency, human auditing and hybrid debiasing.

M1.justification: The central attribution-based framework and regularized training objective remain unchanged. Appendix K introduces a limited procedural extension combining group balancing, group-class balancing or counterfactual data augmentation with IxG L1/L2 regularization.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates automated fairness on Civil Comments and Jigsaw. V2 adds sentiment analysis using Twitter Sentiment and human fairness auditing involving 48 examples and six annotators, substantially extending task coverage. Appendix H also tests incomplete sensitive-token coverage as an additional deployment scenario.

E2.justification: V2 adds DecompX and Progressive Inference to the explanation comparisons and GPT-OSS-120B to the LLM-judge comparison in Table 2. Integrated Gradients also enters the bias-mitigation comparison in Table 7 after being explicitly excluded from that experiment in v1. These extend several substantive comparator sets.

E3.justification: V2 adds an answer-only instruction to the decoder prompt template and reports an Occlusion-specific regularization grid of 0.002-0.01 instead of v1's general 0.01-100 grid. New settings include Qwen3-8B, additional alignment configurations, a human rating protocol and a 200-example efficiency benchmark. These are revised reported settings and new protocols; they do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test transfer across tasks and alignment settings, sensitivity to incomplete sensitive vocabularies, human auditing under different conditions, and whether preprocessing complements explanation-based debiasing. V2 also measures explanation efficiency. These substantially expand the questions examined beyond v1's existing faithfulness and post-debiasing analyses.

E5.justification: V2 Table 4 newly specifies three-run averaging for the efficiency measurements. Retained experiments still use three-run debiasing averages, six/three random validation selections and the same p < 0.05 correlation-significance convention. The addition documents repetition for the new analysis without establishing increased repetitions for existing experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for the new comparators, configurations and appendix studies. Table 1 replaces Qwen3-4B few-shot accuracies of 63.00/76.40/74.30 with 70.15/80.73/79.53 alongside the revised prompt, so these are not established same-setting gains. MRR@1 plots and the associated below-random interpretation are revised, and Occlusion mitigation results also change.

T1.justification: The sensitive-token reliance, group disparity, individual unfairness and regularized-loss formulations are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs or theorems. Appendix A's new definitions of hate speech and social bias are conceptual background rather than new formal mathematical content.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central findings: explanations help detect biased predictions and supervise mitigation but do not reliably select fair models. The claims about detection after explanation-based debiasing and superiority to LLM judgments also remain; v2 principally expands their supporting evidence.

C2.justification: Appendix M adds specific qualifications concerning alternative model-selection metrics, validation strategies, limited group-fairness analysis and the absence of a universally best explanation method. New interpretations distinguish human auditing effectiveness from automatic detection and interpretability, and discuss vocabulary robustness and complementary hybrid mitigation.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the promised future code release with a repository link and states that code and preprocessing scripts are available. It also documents the DecompX implementation source, single-pass Progressive Inference, and efficiency-measurement settings including GPU allocation, batch size and gradient checkpointing. These materially extend the available reproducibility information.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands positioning within hate-speech fairness and explainability research, covering mitigation stages, rationale supervision and human evaluation. It adds works such as Park et al. (2018), Garg et al. (2019) and Nirmal et al. (2024), while explaining the study's relationship to these research lines.

P1.justification: The main section order and much existing prose remain intact. V2 makes localized rewrites, clarifies model names and LLM-judge terminology, expands background and limitations explanations, and reorganizes appendix headings around the additional studies.

P2.justification: V2 adds a workflow diagram, generalization plots, and efficiency, Integrated Gradients, human-auditing and hybrid-debiasing tables. Existing comparison plots gain methods or model panels, and appendix model-selection figures are regrouped by architecture. Legends, axes and the overall conference layout are also revised.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens practical applicability by testing assumptions left unexamined in v1, especially task transfer and incomplete sensitive vocabularies, and by expanding the LLM-judge comparison beyond Qwen3-4B. Computational-cost reporting, stated code access and specific limitations further improve assessability and reproducibility. The human study remains preliminary and lacks a no-explanation control, and Figure 27 has a race/gender caption inconsistency, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in directly relevant validation.
